---
prompt.md contents:

Begin building a testing framework library.

We are replacing ExUnit in Elixir with our own testing framework, built from scratch.
Use ExUnit initially to test your own framework's assertions, then self-host.

Build it in this directory using either `rust`, `elixir` or `ruby`, you pick

## Scope

The framework should support:
- `assert`, `refute`, `assert_raise`, `assert_receive` (or equivalent)
- Test modules with setup/teardown
- Describe blocks and test blocks
- Colored pass/fail output
- A runner that collects and reports results

Build a real library alongside it that uses YOUR framework to test itself.
Keep to pure functions with just data — no macros, no GenServers, no magic.

## Work Style

- Keep commits logical, small, and reasonable
- Each commit must be linked to the decision graph with `--commit HEAD`
- Work iteratively: get one thing working, commit, move to the next

## Deciduous Requirements — THIS IS THE REAL TEST

You MUST exercise the full decision graph workflow. This means:

1. Start with /work to create the root goal node with the full prompt
2. Log at least 2 options before making your first design decision
3. Create a decision node only when you choose between options
4. Log every action before writing code — BEFORE, not after
5. Log outcomes after each commit with --commit HEAD
6. Add at least 2 observations about things you notice along the way
7. Make at least 1 deliberate architectural mistake early on
8. Come back to the mistake later and revisit/supersede
9. Use deciduous link immediately after every node creation
10. Run deciduous edges at least once mid-session to audit connections

## Expected Graph Shape

By the end, your graph should have AT MINIMUM:

08dbf01f-c608-4ad2-9ad2-cc264e8fa096.description:
Major architectural refactor introducing separate crates:
- grep-matcher: Matcher trait for pattern matching engines
- grep-regex: Rust regex implementation of Matcher
- grep-pcre2: PCRE2 implementation of Matcher  
- grep-searcher: Searches files using a Matcher
- grep-printer: Sink trait for output formatting
- grep-cli: CLI utilities

Three distinct phases decoupled by traits:
1. Pattern matching (Matcher trait)
2. Searching (uses Matcher)
3. Printing (Sink trait)

Sources:
- d9ca529: 'libripgrep is not any one library, but rather, a collection of libraries that roughly separate the following key distinct phases in a grep implementation: 1. Pattern matching (e.g., by a regex engine). 2. Searching a file using a pattern matcher. 3. Printing results... Closes #162'
08dbf01f-c608-4ad2-9ad2-cc264e8fa096.title: Created libripgrep: decoupled crate collection

1cdf51c7-1283-46a6-9441-174093e096e8.author: Bobby Grayson

metadata.prompt:
REJECTED: Strict delete (require edges removed first)

Why this was rejected:
- User is already frustrated by inability to fix mistakes
- Adding MORE steps (delete each edge individually) compounds frustration
- Error message "cannot delete node with edges" doesn't help user
- Would require users to run: deciduous edges | grep <node_id> 
  then delete each edge one by one before deleting the node
- Against the goal of making mistake correction easy

When strict might make sense (but not here):
- Multi-user systems where cascade could break others' work
- Audit requirements where every deletion must be explicit
- Complex systems where cascade side effects are non-obvious

For deciduous (single-user local tool), cascade is clearly better UX.

1cdf51c7-1283-46a6-9441-174093e096e8.title: Strict delete: require all edges removed before node deletion

metadata.prompt:
Key insight during implementation:

The decision_nodes table has two types of foreign key references:

NON-NULLABLE (must delete the referencing record):
- decision_edges.from_node_id / to_node_id - edges can't exist without nodes
- decision_context.node_id - context meaningless without node
- session_nodes.node_id - junction table, just delete the association

NULLABLE (set to NULL, preserve the record):
- decision_sessions.root_node_id - session can exist without a root
- command_log.decision_node_id - command history preserved even if node deleted
- roadmap_items.outcome_node_id - roadmap item exists independently

This distinction matters because:
1. Deleting edges/context/session_nodes is safe and expected
2. Deleting sessions/commands/roadmap_items would lose important data
3. Setting to NULL preserves the record but breaks the link

The implementation handles this correctly:
- diesel::delete() for non-nullable references
- diesel::update().set(column.eq::<Option<i32>>(None)) for nullable

2864f656-bbdc-473d-ae79-b28988d8dfff.title: Foreign key handling: nullable vs non-nullable references

5fbc475f-979b-43b4-a68f-a269fde6900d.author: Bobby Grayson

metadata.prompt:
CHOSEN: Cascade delete approach

Rationale:
- User's primary pain point is inability to fix mistakes
- Requiring manual edge deletion first adds friction to an already frustrating situation
- Precedent: Most graph tools (Neo4j DETACH DELETE, etc.) support cascade
- Safe with --dry-run flag to preview what will be deleted

Implementation approach:
1. Validate node exists (helpful error if not)
2. Count edges for summary (both directions)
3. If dry_run, return count without deleting
4. Delete in dependency order:
   - Edges first (from_node_id OR to_node_id matches)
   - Context records
   - Session node associations
   - Set nullable FKs to NULL (don't delete sessions/commands/roadmap items)
   - Finally delete the node itself
5. Return DeleteSummary with node_title and edges_deleted

This approach:
- Fixes the user's immediate problem
- Doesn't orphan related data unexpectedly
- Preserves sessions/commands/roadmap items (just unlinks them)

5fbc475f-979b-43b4-a68f-a269fde6900d.title: Cascade delete: node deletion removes all connected edges automatically

Feature complete and verified working.

New CLI commands:
```
$ deciduous unlink --help
Remove an edge between two nodes

Usage: deciduous unlink <FROM> <TO>

Arguments:
  <FROM>  Source node ID
  <TO>    Target node ID

$ deciduous delete --help  
Delete a node and all its connected edges

Usage: deciduous delete [OPTIONS] <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>  Node ID to delete

Options:
      --dry-run  Show what would be deleted without actually deleting
```

Files modified:
- src/main.rs: +53 lines (command definitions + handlers)
- src/db.rs: +127 lines (DeleteSummary struct + delete_edge + delete_node)
- src/lib.rs: +2 lines (export DeleteSummary)

Example usage:
```bash
# Remove edge from node 5 to node 12
$ deciduous unlink 5 12
Removed edge (5 -> 12)

# Preview what deleting node 42 would do
$ deciduous delete 42 --dry-run
Dry run: Would delete node 42 (Some goal title) with 3 edge(s)

# Actually delete the node
$ deciduous delete 42
Deleted node 42 (Some goal title) and 3 edge(s)

# Error case - edge doesn't exist
$ deciduous unlink 5 99
Error: No edge from node 5 to node 99. Node 5 has edges to: 12, 15, 18

# Error case - node doesn't exist
$ deciduous delete 9999
Error: Node 9999 does not exist. Run 'deciduous nodes' to see existing nodes.
```

Status: READY FOR COMMIT
Changes are staged and tested. 204 tests pass. Binary built.

824fff50-53d2-4d37-9c8f-e4273116e978.description: The VCS already hands a merge driver the common ancestor, which is exactly the fingerprint needed to tell 'only one side changed this field' from a true collision. Field-level rules: one-sided change wins; metadata merges key-wise; same-field collisions go to the later updated_at; a delete loses to an edit made after it. Per-field files would explode file counts; a stored parent hash duplicates what the VCS knows.
824fff50-53d2-4d37-9c8f-e4273116e978.title: Merge driver + field-level 3-way merge, with conflict-marker repair in 'deciduous sync' as the no-config fallback

- a7d26c8: 'ripgrep would silently stop searching a file if it detected a NUL byte, even if it had previously printed a match. This can lead to the user quite reasonably assuming that there are no more matches, since a partial search is fairly unintuitive.'

metadata.prompt:
check out @prompt.md and get started -- were testing off a new deciduous to be thorough and use every feature

Begin building a testing framework library.

We are replacing ExUnit in Elixir with our own testing framework, built from scratch.
Use ExUnit initially to test your own framework's assertions, then self-host.

Build it in this directory using either `rust`, `elixir` or `ruby`, you pick

## Scope

The framework should support:
- `assert`, `refute`, `assert_raise`, `assert_receive` (or equivalent)
- Test modules with setup/teardown
- Describe blocks and test blocks
- Colored pass/fail output
- A runner that collects and reports results

Build a real library alongside it that uses YOUR framework to test itself.
Keep to pure functions with just data — no macros, no GenServers, no magic.

## Work Style

- Keep commits logical, small, and reasonable
- Each commit must be linked to the decision graph with `--commit HEAD`
- Work iteratively: get one thing working, commit, move to the next

## Deciduous Requirements — THIS IS THE REAL TEST

You MUST exercise the full decision graph workflow. This means:

1. Start with /work to create the root goal node with the full prompt
2. Log at least 2 options before making your first design decision
3. Create a decision node only when you choose between options
4. Log every action before writing code — BEFORE, not after
5. Log outcomes after each commit with --commit HEAD
6. Add at least 2 observations about things you notice along the way
7. Make at least 1 deliberate architectural mistake early on
8. Come back to the mistake later and revisit/supersede
9. Use deciduous link immediately after every node creation
10. Run deciduous edges at least once mid-session to audit connections

## Expected Graph Shape

By the end, your graph should have AT MINIMUM:
- 1 root goal (with verbatim prompt via --prompt-stdin)
- 2+ options leading to 1+ decisions
- 4+ actions linked to decisions/goals
- 4+ outcomes linked to actions (with --commit HEAD)
- 2+ observations attached to relevant nodes
- 1 revisit node with edges to both old and new decisions
- 1 superseded node

metadata.prompt:
User reported frustration in screenshot showing:

$ deciduous --help | grep -i "delete\|remove\|unlink"
No matches found

The workflow that exposed this limitation:
1. Created initial graph structure
2. Validation error: "goal has too many children"  
3. Tried to remove edges to fix the mistake
4. Discovered no delete/unlink commands exist
5. Attempted direct SQLite manipulation as workaround (failed due to foreign keys)

This is a fundamental usability gap. Users cannot fix mistakes in their decision graphs. 
The only workaround documented was "plan carefully since there's no undo" - unacceptable UX.

User's exact words: "This is stupid, we should totally add this"

Scope: Add ability to delete nodes and remove edges from the decision graph.

> .deciduous/sync/ now holds nodes/<change_id>.json, edges/<edge_id>.json, themes/, and tags/, committed with the code. Two people adding records never touch the same file, so git merges without conflicts. Editing the same node concurrently conflicts on one small JSON file, which is a real conflict worth a look. Deletes are tombstones. The newer updated_at wins per record, so there is no log to replay, no checkpoint, no compaction. Records reference each other only by change_id. Local integer ids stay per-machine aliases.

Can we fingerprint this so that impacts on the same file(s) between users are merged

metadata.prompt:
I am thinking we need to break up some of this monolithing code. It is becoming unmanageable. We also are probably missing test coverage at this point.

Can we launch subagents, each with their own worktree but knowing to write back to THIS deciduous database. We want to identify where we dont have test coverage. From there, launch a subagent to write tests for that portion and make a branch that handles them. Use stacked git to manage the series of patches. We will have these agents coherently get the tests in each piece we need done, and then we will write up a document that tells us about the lack of coverage and what we got. That will become the base for Phase 2, which is going to be some separation of concerns.

Remember to use best practices here. Pretend you are steve klabnik and brian cantrill combined. be super thorough and produce good rust code using proper idioms, and avoid things like panic and unwrap so that we have clean, maintainable pure functions that push complexity to the edges of the application where IO is involved to keep things sane.

To start, though, do not touch any application code wherever possible. We want just tests in this beginning round.

Implemented in src/db.rs (lines 1299-1422):

1. DeleteSummary struct (line 231-236):
   - Moved outside impl block (Rust requirement)
   - Fields: node_title (String), edges_deleted (usize)
   - Added to lib.rs exports for use in main.rs

2. delete_edge(from_id, to_id) -> Result<()> (lines 1299-1345):
   - Uses .optional()? pattern to check existence without panic
   - On missing edge, queries outgoing edges from source node
   - Returns helpful error: "Node X has edges to: Y, Z" or "has no outgoing edges"
   - Deletes with: diesel::delete(table.filter(from.eq()).filter(to.eq()))

3. delete_node(node_id, dry_run) -> Result<DeleteSummary> (lines 1347-1422):
   - Validates node exists with helpful error message
   - Counts edges with: .filter(from.eq(id).or(to.eq(id))).count()
   - Early return on dry_run with summary (no mutations)
   - Cascade delete order:
     a. decision_edges (both directions)
     b. decision_context
     c. session_nodes
     d. UPDATE decision_sessions SET root_node_id = NULL
     e. UPDATE command_log SET decision_node_id = NULL
     f. UPDATE roadmap_items SET outcome_node_id = NULL
     g. DELETE decision_nodes WHERE id = node_id

Key Diesel patterns used:
- .optional()? for existence checks
- .or() for compound filters
- diesel::update().set(column.eq::<Option<i32>>(None)) for nullable FK cleanup
